value.overview: The White-browed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila bilineata) is a small, active insect-eating songbird of the gnatcatcher family. It was formerly included within the broader Tropical Gnatcatcher complex, but is now recognized as a separate species. It is found from southern Mexico through Central America and south along the Pacific side of the Andes. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of lowland and foothill woodland, forest edges, second growth, scrub, and other partly open habitats.
value.classification: The White-browed Gnatcatcher belongs to the family Polioptilidae, which includes gnatcatchers and gnatwrens. Polioptila bilineata was separated taxonomically from the Tropical Gnatcatcher complex on the basis of plumage, vocalizations, and genetic differences.
value.identification: This is a very small, slender bird with a thin bill, long tail, and restless movements. Adults are mainly blue-gray above and whitish below. The male has a black crown and a conspicuous white eyebrow extending above the eye; the female is generally duller, with less extensive black on the head. The tail is dark with contrasting white outer edges. Its rapid, high-pitched calls and habit of constantly flicking through foliage are useful identification clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, continuing south along the western side of Colombia and Ecuador to Peru. In Costa Rica it occurs on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, especially in lowlands and foothills, and is reported in forest margins, open woodland, second-growth vegetation, scrub, shaded plantations, pastures, and roadside trees. It is less common in the dry northwest than in many other parts of the country and is usually found below about 1,200 meters.
value.migrationStatus: White-browed Gnatcatchers are generally resident rather than migratory. Individuals remain in Costa Rica throughout the year, although local movements may occur in response to food availability, weather, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding involves a small, compact cup nest made from plant fibers and other fine materials, often secured with spider webbing in a tree or large shrub. The nest is typically placed at low or middle height, though placement varies with habitat. Both members of a pair may participate in territory defense and reproductive activities. Breeding timing can vary geographically and is associated with local rainy-season conditions and food availability.
value.dietFeeding: The White-browed Gnatcatcher feeds mainly on small arthropods, including insects, insect larvae, and spiders. It usually gleans prey from leaves, twigs, and branches while moving rapidly through the canopy, woodland edge, or shrub layer. It may also make short flights to capture flying insects. Pairs or small family groups often forage actively together, pausing frequently to give soft contact calls.
value.behavior: This species is energetic, alert, and usually seen in pairs or family groups. It moves quickly through foliage with frequent tail flicking and short hops between branches. Although it often forages above ground, it may descend into dense shrubs or low vegetation in open habitats. Its voice consists of thin, rapid notes and trills. Pairs commonly maintain territories year-round, and the birds can be conspicuous despite their small size because of their constant activity.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread, and no well-established evidence indicates a major global population decline.
